fuente.nota: Text shortened by paragraphs; sentences unchanged.

parrafos: A school is an educational learning institution designed to provide classes and learning environment to teach students, usually with help of a teacher or professor. Some senior secondary schools can also be considered as a college. Almost all countries and states have systems of formal education, which is sometimes compulsory or legally required. There are various types of schools or learning programs. Topics such as reading, writing, and mathematics are central to education for children.

Most of a student's time is spent in a classroom. This is where 10 to 30 people sit to take part in educational discussion. In the United States, the average number of students per classroom in primary schools is 23.1.

The term "school" is used for many educational environments – particularly in North America. In North America, a person taking a first degree at a university is often self-described as "going to school". In Europe that would never be the case. They would describe themselves as "going to university". The style of university education can be so different between countries.

In many places around the world, children must go to school for a certain number of years. Learning may take place in the classroom, in outside environments, or on visits to other places. Colleges and universities are places to learn for students over 17 or 18 years of age. Vocational schools teach skills people need for jobs.

Some people attend school longer than others. This is because some jobs require more training than others, like for example becoming a doctor takes about 10-14 years of education. For young children, one teacher may teach all subjects. Teachers for older students are more specialized, and they only teach a few subjects. Common subjects taught include science, arts such as music, humanities, like geography and history, and languages.

Children with mental health problems, and problems such as autism and other conditions, usually do not go to regular classrooms. These children are given other ways to get schooling, like special classrooms or even special schools. There also are special schools which teach things which regular schools do not, such as how to walk or read braille.
Graduate schools are in universities. They are for students who have graduated with a first degree from colleges and universities. The aim is to offer Masters and PhD courses to the best students.

Education for all is quite modern. In England, for example, most men could not read or write, even early in the 19th century. We know this because when they got married, those who could not write put an 'X' on the certificate, and someone else wrote down their name. At the time, most women could write, because they stayed at home. Widespread education for reading and writing began in the 19th century.
Long ago, most schools were run by religious denominations. That is because clerics were once almost the only people who were literate: they were able to read and write.

In most countries, boys were taught differently to girls, and separately from girls. Today, most countries have schools which accept both boys and girls, though some places still have separate schools for girls. Some parents believe that girls do better in schools with only one gender.

Pedagogy is the science of teaching children. Different schools use different ways of teaching. There is quite a lot of disagreement about what and how students should be taught. Many countries solve this by allowing different types of schools, so parents and children have some choice. Choices may include home education, which is a controversial idea. Few people do this. Even in pre-modern times, most children were taught in groups. Age grouping is also ancient. It was done in many African tribes for a long time before the present.

A British term which means roughly "a secondary school for all children in a particular neighbourhood". It includes the idea of taking both boys and girls in one school, and the idea of taking children of all abilities. In practice it has many of the problems which are endemic in American high schools. Among its main faults are said to be: putting girls and boys together at the sensitive time of puberty, and the behavioural problems associated with having such a wide range of young people in a large school. Evidence for lowered standards for examinations are disputed, but widely believed to be true.

Boarding schools are schools where children are sent to live on a school campus without their parents. They are expensive, and so are chosen by parents with means. They are not for the average family. They are usually elite schools with the best teachers that money can buy. Children may even be sent to another country. Switzerland is one of the favoured countries. On the other hand, most Western countries have first-rate boarding schools. In England, many public schools are boarding schools. The term "public school" here has a special meaning: it really means "private school".

"Preparatory schoolboys live in a world completely dissociated from home life. They have a different vocabulary, a different moral system, even different voices. On their return to school from the holidays the change-over from home-self to school-self is almost instantaneous, whereas the reverse process takes a fortnight at least. A preparatory schoolboy, when caught off his guard, will call his mother 'Please, matron,' and always addresses any male relative or friend of the family as 'Sir', like a master. I used to do it".

resumen_es: An informative text about what a school is, the different types of school (vocational, special, graduate, mixed, comprehensive and boarding schools) and the historical development of universal education.
nivel_motivo: Although the vocabulary is simple, the text includes terms such as “denominations”, “endemic” or “pedagogy” and a final literary quotation that place it above A2.

ideas_clave.idea: A school is an institution where teachers instruct pupils, and most countries have formal, often mandatory, education systems centred on literacy and numeracy.
Pupils spend most of their time in classrooms, and the word 'school' has a broader meaning in North America, where it also covers university studies.
The length of schooling varies with the training a career demands, and teachers become more specialised as students grow older, from compulsory school to university and vocational training.
Special schools cater for children with particular needs, while graduate schools within universities offer master's and doctoral programmes.
Universal education is a recent development: mass literacy only spread in the nineteenth century, and earlier schooling was mostly in the hands of religious bodies.
Boys and girls were traditionally educated apart; mixed schools now prevail, although single-sex schools survive.
Since there is little agreement on teaching methods, many countries let families choose between different kinds of schools, including the controversial option of home education.
British comprehensive schools admit all local children regardless of sex or ability, but they are criticised for behavioural problems and possibly lower standards.
Boarding schools are costly elite institutions where pupils live away from home, an experience that shapes a separate 'school self', as a former pupil's testimony shows.

resumen_modelo: The text describes the school as an institution in which teachers instruct pupils within formal education systems that are, in many countries, compulsory and focused on basic skills such as reading, writing and arithmetic. It notes that the word has a wider meaning in North America, where even university students say they are 'going to school'. The duration of studies depends on the demands of each profession, and whereas young children usually have a single teacher, older pupils are taught by specialists. Alongside ordinary schools, there are vocational centres, special schools for children with particular needs and graduate schools offering postgraduate degrees. Historically, however, education for all is a fairly recent achievement: literacy only became widespread in the nineteenth century, and before that most schools were run by religious institutions. Similarly, boys and girls used to be taught separately, although mixed schools are now the norm. Because there is considerable debate about how children should be taught, many countries offer families a choice of schools. Two British models are examined in particular: comprehensive schools, which admit all local pupils but are blamed for discipline problems and falling standards, and expensive boarding schools, where children live away from their families and develop a distinct identity.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: In US primary schools, there are on average about 23 pupils per class.
preguntas.cita: In the United States, the average number of students per classroom in primary schools is 23.1.
preguntas.explicacion: The text gives exactly the figure of 23.1 pupils per class in primary school in the United States, which rounds to 23.

preguntas.pregunta: According to the text, how would a European university student describe what they do?
opciones: As 'taking a first degree at school'
preguntas.cita: In Europe that would never be the case. They would describe themselves as "going to university".
preguntas.explicacion: The text contrasts North American usage (“going to school”) with European usage (“going to university”). “Going to college” is not mentioned, and the first option is precisely the usage that the text attributes to North America.

preguntas.enunciado: Find in paragraph 3 a word meaning “related to training for a trade or profession”.
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning 'related to the skills needed for a particular job'.
preguntas.cita: Vocational schools teach skills people need for jobs.
preguntas.explicacion: “Vocational” refers to training for a job (es: formación profesional); in Spanish, “escuelas de formación profesional”. Careful: it does not mean “vocacional” in the religious sense.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Becoming a doctor takes around 6 to 8 years of education.
preguntas.cita: becoming a doctor takes about 10-14 years of education
preguntas.explicacion: The text talks about some 10 to 14 years of training to become a doctor, not 6 to 8.

preguntas.pregunta: Which of the following is mentioned as something special schools may teach?
opciones: How to speak a foreign language
preguntas.cita: There also are special schools which teach things which regular schools do not, such as how to walk or read braille.
preguntas.explicacion: The text mentions walking and reading Braille. Sign language is not mentioned, and music and languages appear as common subjects in ordinary schools, not in special schools.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: In early nineteenth-century England, most women were also unable to write.
preguntas.cita: At the time, most women could write, because they stayed at home.
preguntas.explicacion: According to the text, most men could not write, but most women could, because they stayed at home.

preguntas.enunciado: Find in paragraph 8 a word meaning “able to read and write”.
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning 'able to read and write'.
preguntas.cita: clerics were once almost the only people who were literate: they were able to read and write.
preguntas.explicacion: “Literate” means able to read and write (es: alfabetizado); the text itself explains it straight afterwards (“able to read and write”). Its opposite is “illiterate”.

preguntas.pregunta: Why were most schools once run by religious groups?
opciones: Because governments refused to pay for education
Because clerics were almost the only literate people
Because parents preferred a religious education
Because schools were built inside churches
respuestas: Because clerics were almost the only literate people
preguntas.cita: That is because clerics were once almost the only people who were literate
preguntas.explicacion: The text puts it down to the fact that clerics were almost the only people who could read and write. The other reasons (public funding, parents’ preferences, buildings) are not mentioned.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Studies prove that girls achieve better results in single-sex schools.
preguntas.explicacion: The text only says that some parents believe it (“Some parents believe”), but it does not mention any studies that prove it.

preguntas.pregunta: How do many countries deal with disagreement about teaching methods, and what example of a controversial option does the text give?
respuestas: They allow different types of schools to exist so that parents and children can choose. Home education is given as an example of a controversial choice, which few people make.
preguntas.cita: Many countries solve this by allowing different types of schools, so parents and children have some choice.
preguntas.explicacion: The answer should cover the solution (a variety of schools and freedom of choice) and the example of home schooling, described as controversial and uncommon.

preguntas.enunciado: Find in paragraph 11 a word meaning “common and deeply rooted in a place or group” (synonym: widespread).
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning 'regularly found within a particular place or group'.
preguntas.cita: In practice it has many of the problems which are endemic in American high schools.
preguntas.explicacion: “Endemic” describes something typical and persistent in a place; here, problems typical of American high schools.

preguntas.pregunta: Which criticism of comprehensive schools does the text mention?
opciones: They are too expensive for average families
They mix boys and girls during puberty
They only admit the most able pupils
They are run by religious organisations
respuestas: They mix boys and girls during puberty
preguntas.cita: putting girls and boys together at the sensitive time of puberty
preguntas.explicacion: One of the criticisms mentioned is putting boys and girls together during puberty. High cost refers to boarding schools, and comprehensive schools admit pupils of all abilities, not only the best.

preguntas.pregunta: Why might the expression 'public school' be confusing in England?
respuestas: Because in England a 'public school' is actually a private, fee-paying school, often a boarding school, which is the opposite of what the term suggests elsewhere.
preguntas.cita: The term "public school" here has a special meaning: it really means "private school".
preguntas.explicacion: This is a usage specific to British English: “public school” refers to elite private schools, not state schools.

preguntas.pregunta: What does the quotation in the last paragraph suggest about the experience of boarding-school pupils?
respuestas: It suggests that boarders live in a world separate from their family life, with their own language and values, and adapt so deeply to school that they find it hard to switch back to their home identity, even calling their mother 'matron'.
preguntas.cita: Preparatory schoolboys live in a world completely dissociated from home life.
preguntas.explicacion: The quotation shows the boarder’s double identity: the switch to the “school identity” is immediate, while going back to the “home identity” takes at least a fortnight.
